segments.desc: Civic-minded transparency advocates who believe government should be accountable to citizens and strongly support public access to budget information as a fundamental right of democratic participation.
Pragmatic reformers who support public access to budgets and expenditures as a way to reduce corruption and improve government efficiency, viewing transparency as a practical governance tool.

Traditional authority respecters who are uncertain about public budget disclosure, viewing government as an institution that should maintain some discretion, though they may lean toward transparency if convinced it serves community interests.

Skeptical disengaged citizens who doubt government will share information anyway or believe such transparency efforts are futile given low government responsiveness, so they remain indifferent to the question.
Government confidentiality supporters who believe certain budget and expenditure details should remain restricted to government use for security, administrative, or hierarchical reasons.

Deeply dissatisfied critics who see government failure across the board. They believe health facilities are severely under-resourced and point to broader patterns of poor economic management and service delivery as evidence.

Moderately dissatisfied skeptics who acknowledge some government effort but see significant gaps in health facility resources. They are somewhat cynical about government capacity based on mixed COVID-19 relief experiences.

Cautiously satisfied pragmatists who recognize constraints and see some improvement in health facility preparedness, though they wish for more. They tend to give the government partial credit for efforts made.

Supportive optimists who are fairly or very satisfied with government's health facility resource allocation during COVID-19. They believe the government has done reasonably well under difficult circumstances.

Disengaged or uncertain citizens who lack strong opinions or sufficient information to judge government performance on health facility resources. They may refuse to answer or admit they don't know enough.

Disconnected and distrustful citizens who have never contacted their local councillor and see little point in doing so, given widespread skepticism about government responsiveness and accessibility to information.

Economically struggling citizens who occasionally reach out to councillors about urgent problems like cash income or healthcare needs, driven by desperation rather than confidence in government effectiveness.

Civically engaged citizens who contact their councillor a few times per year to advocate for local development and hold government accountable, believing in the importance of public participation despite frustrations.
Active community advocates who frequently engage with their local councillor on multiple issues, maintaining hope that persistent engagement can drive change and improve local governance.
Uncertain citizens who are unsure whether they have ever contacted a councillor or cannot recall, reflecting broader confusion about local government structures and processes.

Cautiously optimistic civic participants who believe local government is reasonably accessible and responsive; they have moderate trust in institutions and expect they could obtain budget and development information with some effort.

Skeptical but engaged citizens who doubt government transparency and worry about bureaucratic obstacles; they think getting local development and budget information would be difficult despite believing it should be public.

Confident institutional believers with high trust in traditional and local leadership structures; they expect local government would readily share development plans and budget information if asked directly.
Disengaged or pessimistic individuals who have little faith in government responsiveness and believe local officials would not provide budget or development information even if requested.
Uncertain or uninformed citizens who haven't had enough direct experience with local government institutions to judge whether they could access development plans and budget information.

Democratic institutionalists who strongly value civilian governance and parliamentary democracy, having witnessed the importance of elected representatives despite current dissatisfaction with Parliament's performance.

Pragmatic governance-focused citizens who are frustrated with current political institutions but cautious about military rule, preferring to work within existing democratic systems despite their flaws.

Stability-seeking individuals who are open to military intervention as a potential solution to governance problems, viewing the army as a possible alternative to what they see as ineffective civilian leadership.

Deeply disillusioned citizens with low confidence in all institutions—both civilian and military—who neither approve nor disapprove of military governance, seeing little meaningful difference between alternatives.
Uncertain or disengaged respondents who lack sufficient knowledge or interest in governance structures to form strong opinions about military rule.
Skeptical of government institutions who doubt the government's capacity or willingness to ensure vaccine safety, given widespread perceptions of corruption and presidential overreach.
Cautiously trusting citizens who have some confidence in the government's vaccine safety processes but remain somewhat uncertain given mixed experiences with public health responses.

Moderately confident supporters who trust the government to ensure vaccine safety, reflecting the pattern of qualified faith in institutions seen in responses about traditional leaders and health facility resources.
Uninformed or undecided respondents who lack sufficient knowledge about government vaccine safety protocols to form a clear opinion.

Strong government skeptics who have little to no trust in the government's ability to prioritize citizen safety over other interests, aligned with the 63% who see corruption as having increased significantly.
Economically distressed citizens who blame the government for poor economic management and see the country heading in the wrong direction. This group is deeply pessimistic about national prospects.

Skeptical moderates who acknowledge government failures in COVID relief and economic management but haven't fully decided on the country's overall trajectory. They are uncertain but lean toward concern.

Civic-minded citizens who support transparency and accountability in government, and who view corruption as widespread among elites. They see systemic problems suggesting the country is going in the wrong direction.

Cautiously optimistic citizens who recognize current challenges but believe the country can improve or has some positive elements worth preserving. They are more likely to see potential for the right direction.
Disengaged or uncertain respondents who lack sufficient information about government performance or national direction to form strong opinions. They may refuse to answer or express uncertainty.

Optimistic progressives (urban, educated, younger): Believe that running for office would enhance a woman's standing in the community, viewing political participation as a path to respect and social advancement.
Cautious moderates (mixed urban-rural, moderate education): Think it's somewhat likely a woman candidate would gain standing, but recognize this depends heavily on local attitudes and family support.

Traditional skeptics (rural, older, more conservative): Doubt that a woman running for office would significantly improve her family's standing, believing traditional gender roles and community hierarchies remain strong.

Pessimistic realists (aware of gender barriers): Believe it's unlikely a woman candidate would gain standing, viewing entrenched gender discrimination and social resistance as too strong to overcome through political candidacy.
Uncertain respondents: Lack sufficient exposure to or experience with women in politics to form a clear opinion on whether candidacy would improve community standing.

Conservative traditionalists who strongly oppose immigration and foreign workers, viewing them as threats to local employment and cultural values. This group shows the same pattern of strong rejection seen toward homosexuals.
Pragmatic moderates who somewhat dislike immigrants or foreign workers due to economic concerns, but are not strongly opposed and recognize some potential benefits.
Cosmopolitan urbanites and business-oriented individuals who are indifferent to immigrants and foreign workers, viewing them as a normal part of economic life.
Progressive-minded citizens who somewhat like or appreciate immigrants and foreign workers for their contributions to the economy and cultural diversity.
A small segment of strongly pro-immigration advocates who value diversity and see foreign workers as beneficial to national development.

Disillusioned critics who see Parliament as ineffective and corrupt, viewing MPs as failing to represent their interests or address economic hardship. They strongly disapprove of parliamentary performance.

Moderately dissatisfied citizens who acknowledge some parliamentary effort but believe MPs are underperforming given Nigeria's economic challenges and widespread corruption. They disapprove but not strongly.

Cautiously optimistic supporters who believe Parliament is making reasonable efforts despite systemic constraints, or who have limited information but give the benefit of the doubt. They approve of parliamentary performance.
Partisan strong supporters who view their MPs favorably, perhaps seeing them as working within difficult circumstances or aligned with their political preferences. They strongly approve.
Uncertain or disengaged citizens who lack sufficient information about parliamentary performance to form a clear judgment. They haven't heard enough to say.

Literal Causality Reasoners (45%): These workers focus on which hypothesis directly causes the outcome. They recognize that Hypothesis-1 (hiking at night) is illogical and counterproductive for completing a hike, while Hypothesis-2 (a warning about a fawn) is a plausible obstacle that could be overcome, making it the more relevant cause.

Outcome-Focused Pragmatists (35%): These workers reason backward from the ending to determine which hypothesis better explains how Tom succeeded. They see that a ranger's warning is a concrete event that could lead to Tom adjusting his approach and finishing anyway, whereas hiking in darkness seems unrelated to success.

Logical Consistency Checkers (12%): These workers evaluate hypotheses for internal coherence with the beginning and ending. They notice that Hypothesis-1 contradicts normal hiking practices and the goal of completing a hike, making Hypothesis-2 the only logically consistent option.

Contrarian Literalists (5%): These workers occasionally select Hypothesis-1 by interpreting the question in unconventional ways or by focusing on technical wording rather than narrative logic, though this approach conflicts with the group's strong pattern.

Uncertain Reasoners (3%): These workers struggle to distinguish between the hypotheses and may randomly select or be genuinely confused about the causal relationship, representing the small margin of inconsistency in group responses.
Literal interpreters who focus on precise language. They note that 'standing on a roof' contradicts 'under a thatched roof' (being underneath vs. on top), making the statement definitely incorrect.

Flexible readers who see 'under a thatched roof' as describing a covered structure where people gather, and interpret 'standing on a roof' as a reasonable paraphrase of people being in/at that roofed location, viewing it as definitely correct.
Cautious moderates who recognize the ambiguity in spatial language and the possibility of different interpretations, settling on neither definitely correct nor incorrect as the safest judgment.

Detail-focused skeptics who note that while both involve roofs and groups of men, the specific spatial relationship (under vs. on) and the lack of explicit confirmation that they're standing creates enough uncertainty to lean toward incorrect.
Pragmatic readers who accept minor variations in description as acceptable paraphrasing, viewing the core claim (men at a roof structure) as essentially correct despite imprecise wording.

Literal interpreters who focus on the definition provided. They see the statement as making a claim about general administrative preferences that goes beyond the narrow definition of budgetary resources given, so they view it as neither definitely correct nor incorrect based solely on the context.

Strict definitional readers who believe the statement introduces new information (administrative preferences) not contained in the definition itself. They tend to mark this as definitely incorrect because the context only defines what budgetary resources are, not how administrations feel about distributing them.

Pragmatic reasoners who recognize that the statement is a reasonable inference from understanding what budgetary resources are—if agencies have different resource needs and capabilities, it logically follows that some should have more. They lean toward marking it as definitely correct.

Cautious agnostics who acknowledge the statement could be true in practice but recognize it's not explicitly stated or logically entailed by the definition alone. They default to the middle category as the safest choice.

Context-skeptics who view any statement extending beyond the immediate definition as overreach. They mark it as definitely incorrect because the definition is purely technical and makes no claims about administrative preferences or policy decisions.

Strict Literalists - These workers interpret 'many tapes' as requiring explicit confirmation of quantity in the source material. Since the title only mentions tapes exist but doesn't specify 'many,' they see this as not definitely correct.

Reasonable Inferrers - These workers view the title 'Inside the Oval White House Tapes From FDR to Clinton' as clearly implying multiple tapes across many presidencies, making 'many tapes' a reasonable inference that counts as definitely correct.

Cautious Moderates - These workers recognize that while tapes clearly existed and the title suggests multiple ones, the word 'many' is somewhat subjective and the context doesn't explicitly quantify them, so they default to the neither/nor category.

Skeptical Readers - These workers focus on the distinction between the title describing a book about tapes versus confirming that many tapes were actually taken, viewing this as an unwarranted leap from the source material.

Pragmatic Acceptors - These workers see 'many' as a natural reading of a title spanning multiple presidencies (FDR to Clinton) and consider the statement definitely correct based on common sense interpretation.

Literal interpreters who focus on direct causality. They see Hypothesis-1 as more plausible because the shop visit directly enables finding a gift for a friend, making it the clearer causal path to the ending.

Motivation-focused reasoners who prioritize intent and personal desire. They believe Hypothesis-2 (wanting a gift for herself) is more plausible because self-interest typically drives shopping behavior, even if the outcome happens to benefit a friend.
Outcome-agnostic skeptics who see both hypotheses as equally weak explanations. They recognize that neither hypothesis strongly predicts finding a gift for a friend, making this question ambiguous.

Context-sensitive readers who note the contradiction in Hypothesis-2. They find Hypothesis-1 more plausible because wanting a gift for oneself contradicts the ending where she finds a gift for her friend.

Pragmatic reasoners who consider real-world shopping patterns. They lean toward Hypothesis-1 because people shopping in gift shops are typically looking for presents for others, making this the most realistic scenario.
Strict Literalists - These workers require direct, explicit confirmation in the context. Since the context mentions train tracks but not a bridge, they view the statement as definitely incorrect.

Contextual Reasoners - These workers recognize that train tracks in a large city could plausibly be viewed from a bridge, making the statement neither definitely correct nor incorrect based on the given information.
Generous Interpreters - These workers see the statement as potentially correct since bridges commonly overlook train tracks in urban areas, and the context is compatible with this scenario.
Uncertain Skeptics - These workers lean toward the statement being incorrect because the context specifically says 'train tracks' without mentioning a bridge, but they acknowledge some ambiguity.

Pragmatic Moderates - These workers default to option C when there's any reasonable doubt, viewing most statements as neither definitely correct nor incorrect unless there's clear contradiction or confirmation.

Narrative Logic Followers (45%): These workers focus on what logically resolves the narrative tension. They recognize that Tom's belief in being amazing is contradicted by losing to his dad, making Hypothesis-2 the clear causal mechanism for his humbling realization.

Outcome-Focused Reasoners (35%): These workers identify which hypothesis directly explains the O-Ending's emotional content. They see that losing (Hypothesis-2) directly causes amazement and humbling, while winning (Hypothesis-1) would not produce this outcome.

Literal Interpretation Skeptics (12%): These workers question whether either hypothesis perfectly fits, noting that Hypothesis-1 could also lead to humbling if Tom's dad was previously unknown to be skilled. They may hesitate between options but lean toward Hypothesis-2 as more direct.

Contrarian Readers (5%): These workers interpret Hypothesis-1 charitably, suggesting that Tom's amazement at his dad's inability to beat him could lead to humbling through overconfidence backfiring. They represent the small minority who might choose Hypothesis-1.

Pattern Matchers (3%): These workers apply the strong pattern from previous questions where the hypothesis that directly contradicts or undermines the O-Beginning is correct. They automatically select Hypothesis-2 without deep narrative analysis.

Literal interpreters who focus on exact wording: These workers notice that the statement uses 'because' to establish causation, while the context uses 'equate with' to describe an assumption, making them logically different claims. They would likely choose (B) or (C).

Semantic paraphrasers who see the core meaning as equivalent: These workers view the statement as a reasonable paraphrase of the speaker's point about the automatic equation between income and education, treating them as essentially the same idea. They would likely choose (A).

Cautious middle-grounders who recognize ambiguity in speaker intent: These workers acknowledge that while the statement captures part of what was said, the original phrasing is more about perception/assumption than about actual causation, making it neither fully correct nor incorrect. They would choose (C).

Critical readers who distinguish between describing a bias and endorsing it: These workers note that the context describes people making an automatic equation (a bias), while the statement could be read as endorsing that equation as fact, making them meaningfully different. They would choose (B).

Pragmatic interpreters focused on conversational intent: These workers see the speaker as expressing skepticism about the automatic equation itself, and view the statement as misrepresenting this skepticism as a straightforward claim. They would choose (B).

Literal Interpreters (35%): These workers focus strictly on what is explicitly stated in the context. Since the context only mentions 'Receiving Water Samples' as a heading/label without describing an actual action or requirement, they see the statement as neither definitely correct nor incorrect—it's a restatement of the label without confirmation of necessity.

Procedural Reasoners (25%): These workers interpret the context as describing a procedural step in a process. They view the statement as definitely correct because 'Receiving Water Samples' as a section heading logically implies that water samples should indeed be received as part of that procedure.

Strict Contradiction Seekers (15%): These workers look for direct contradictions between context and statement. Finding none here, they default to the uncertain category, similar to how they handle ambiguous cases where the statement doesn't directly contradict the context.

Cautious Skeptics (20%): These workers are hesitant to affirm statements without explicit confirmation in the context. They recognize the statement could be true but see insufficient evidence to call it 'definitely correct,' placing it in the neither/nor category as a safe middle ground.

Semantic Doubters (5%): These workers question whether a procedural heading necessarily implies the action should occur, viewing the statement as potentially incorrect or at least not definitively supported by a mere section title.

Literal Readers: These workers carefully parse the logical relationship between context and statement. They recognize that the context discusses regulatory comment procedures while the statement makes a sweeping political claim, finding no direct connection and selecting (C).

Strict Falsifiers: These workers view the statement as making a definitive claim about voting efficacy that contradicts the context's implicit assumption that public participation (comments) matters in governance, leading them to select (B).

Charitable Interpreters: These workers attempt to find some thematic link between civic engagement (the context) and voting (the statement), and while skeptical, see enough ambiguity to select (C) rather than commit to definite incorrectness.
Cynical Validators: These workers agree with the sentiment of the statement and see it as expressing a reasonable political viewpoint, selecting (A) despite weak contextual support.
Uncertain Moderates: These workers are genuinely unsure how to categorize the relationship and default to (C) as the safest middle ground when context and statement seem unrelated.

Risk-averse maximizers who prefer guaranteed negative outcomes over gambles with high loss probability. They choose Machine A because -$3 is certain and better than the 75% chance of -$11, even though Machine B has upside potential.
Expected value calculators who recognize that Machine B has a positive expected value (-$11×0.75 + $20×0.25 = -$6.25 vs -$3) and choose it despite the risk, focusing on long-term optimization.
Upside-focused optimists who are drawn to Machine B's $20 potential payoff and the 25% chance of a positive bonus, willing to accept the 75% loss probability for the possibility of a gain.

Loss-minimizers who recognize that Machine A guarantees a $0 bonus (since negative rewards yield $0 bonus) while Machine B offers only a small chance of a positive bonus, making Machine A the safer choice.
Inconsistent decision-makers who apply different heuristics across similar problems, sometimes choosing guaranteed losses and sometimes gambling, reflecting uncertainty about their own preferences.
Expected value maximizers who calculate the mathematical expectation of each option and choose accordingly. Machine A has an expected value of $30.99 while Machine B has $39.50, so they choose B.

Risk-averse players who prefer certainty and stable outcomes, favoring Machine A because it guarantees $30 with only a small 1% chance of a better outcome, viewing the guaranteed income as more valuable than chasing higher variance.

Upside-focused optimists who are drawn to the possibility of larger payoffs and choose Machine B for its higher expected value and better worst-case scenario ($34 vs $30), seeing it as the smarter bet.

Loss-minimizers who focus on avoiding the worst outcomes and choose Machine A because even though Machine B has better expected value, they dislike the 25% chance of getting only $34 when they could guarantee $30 with near certainty.
Inconsistent decision-makers who don't apply a consistent strategy across similar problems and may choose either option based on framing or intuition rather than systematic analysis.

Expected value maximizers who calculate the mathematical expectation of each option and choose accordingly. Machine A gives $12 with certainty, while Machine B has an expected value of $12.50 (0.25×$8 + 0.50×$14 + 0.25×$12), so they choose Machine B.

Risk-averse individuals who prefer certainty and guaranteed outcomes over gambles with similar or slightly higher expected values. They choose Machine A because it guarantees $12 with no downside risk.
Moderate risk-takers who recognize that Machine B offers a small expected value advantage ($0.50) and are willing to accept the variance for a chance at $14, choosing Machine B.
Individuals who focus on the upside potential and are attracted to the possibility of winning $14 from Machine B, even though it means accepting some downside risk compared to the guaranteed $12.
Inconsistent or random decision-makers who don't apply a consistent strategy across similar problems, making choices that vary unpredictably between the two options.
Expected value maximizers who calculate the mathematical expectation for each machine and choose accordingly. Machine A has EV of $29.4 while Machine B has EV of $25, so they choose A.

Risk-averse players who prefer guaranteed or highly probable positive outcomes and avoid machines with significant downside risk. They choose Machine A because it offers 90% certainty of a good outcome versus the 50% chance of losing $9 with Machine B.

Upside-focused gamblers who are attracted to the possibility of larger payoffs and are willing to tolerate downside risk. They choose Machine B because the $59 potential reward is substantially higher than Machine A's maximum of $30.

Inconsistent decision-makers who sometimes focus on expected value, sometimes on risk, and sometimes on maximum payoff, leading to variable choices across similar problems. They are split between both options.

Loss-averse players who are particularly sensitive to the possibility of negative outcomes and strongly prefer machines that cannot produce losses. They choose Machine A to avoid the $9 loss possibility entirely.
Expected value maximizers who calculate the mathematical expectation of each machine and choose accordingly. Machine A has EV of $11.20 while Machine B has EV of $9.03, so they choose Machine A.

Risk-averse players who prefer machines with more consistent, predictable payouts and lower variance. They favor Machine A because it has only two outcomes with a high probability of a modest gain, avoiding the complexity and negative outcome in Machine B.
Complexity-averse decision makers who are overwhelmed by Machine B's seven different outcomes and probabilities. They default to the simpler Machine A as the easier choice to understand and evaluate.

Upside-focused optimists who are attracted to Machine B's potential for higher payouts (up to $12.50) despite the negative outcome, believing the diversified options offer better opportunities than Machine A's capped maximum of $28.

Loss-averse players who are particularly concerned about Machine B's -$7.0 outcome and the 20% chance of losing money. They strongly prefer Machine A's guaranteed positive outcomes, even though the math slightly favors Machine A anyway.
Expected value maximizers who calculate the mathematical expectation for each machine and choose accordingly. Machine A has EV of -9.25, Machine B has EV of -23.2, so they choose Machine A.
Risk-seeking gamblers who are attracted to the possibility of a large positive payoff ($97) despite the low probability and negative expected value, choosing Machine B for the upside potential.
Loss-averse decision makers who focus on minimizing the worst-case scenario. They see Machine A's maximum loss of -13 as better than Machine B's -28, choosing Machine A.
Probability-focused individuals who notice Machine B's 90% chance of a large loss and view this as unacceptably risky, preferring Machine A's more predictable negative outcomes.
Inconsistent or random responders who don't apply consistent decision logic across similar problems, making unpredictable choices.

Expected value maximizers who calculate the mathematical expectation for each machine and choose accordingly. Machine A has EV of 0.25(-9) + 0.75(23) = 15.75; Machine B has EV of 0.60(-7) + 0.40(51) = 16.8, so they choose B.

Risk-averse players who prefer the machine with higher probability of a positive outcome and more stable returns, favoring Machine A's 75% chance of winning $23 over Machine B's 40% chance despite slightly lower expected value.
Upside-focused gamblers attracted to Machine B's higher maximum payoff ($51 vs $23) and willing to accept the higher loss probability for the chance at a bigger win.

Loss-averse decision makers who are particularly concerned about avoiding the worst-case scenarios and choose Machine A because its minimum loss of -$9 is smaller than Machine B's -$7 in absolute terms, or focus on the higher win probability.
Inconsistent or random responders who don't apply a consistent decision rule and may choose based on intuition, framing effects, or other non-systematic factors.
Expected value maximizers who calculate the mathematical expectation for each machine and choose accordingly. Machine B has an expected value of $5.90 vs Machine A's $5.00, so they choose B.
Risk-averse players who prefer certainty and guaranteed outcomes. They choose Machine A because it guarantees $5.00 with no downside risk, even though the expected value is slightly lower.
Upside-focused optimists who are attracted to the possibility of higher payoffs. They choose Machine B because the chance to win $8.00 appeals to them more than the guaranteed $5.00.
Indifferent or random responders who see the two options as essentially similar since both are positive and low-risk, so they pick either option without strong conviction.
Bonus-focused thinkers who recognize that since negative outcomes are zeroed out, they should focus on maximizing positive expected bonuses. They choose Machine B for its higher expected value.
Expected value maximizers who calculate the mathematical expectation for each machine and choose accordingly. Machine A has EV of $28.4 while Machine B has EV of $26.2, so they choose Machine A.
Risk-averse players who prefer certainty and stable outcomes, favoring Machine B's 95% chance of $27 over Machine A's volatile 60/40 split with a large negative outcome.
Loss-averse decision makers who are particularly sensitive to the -$32 downside in Machine A and choose Machine B to avoid the possibility of a significant loss.
Upside-focused optimists who are attracted to Machine A's $71 potential reward and believe the 60% probability of winning makes it worth the risk despite the downside.
Uncertain or indifferent players who find the choice difficult and could reasonably go either way, perhaps slightly leaning toward the safer Machine B option.

Expected value maximizers who calculate the mathematical expectation for each machine and choose accordingly. Machine A gives $20 with certainty (EV=$20), while Machine B has EV=$20.15, so they choose B.

Risk-averse players who prefer certainty and guaranteed outcomes. They see Machine A's guaranteed $20 as clearly superior to Machine B's uncertain distribution with similar expected value, so they choose A.
Upside-focused optimists attracted to the possibility of winning $33.50 or $34.50 on Machine B, viewing the higher ceiling as worth the risk despite the lower probability, so they choose B.

Loss-averse decision makers who focus on downside protection. They note Machine B has a 10% chance of only $18 (below the guaranteed $20), making them uncomfortable with that tail risk, so they choose A.
Indifferent or uncertain reasoners who see the machines as roughly equivalent in value and either flip a mental coin or lack strong conviction, splitting between A and B.
Skeptical rationalists who trust scientific consensus and institutional authority. They are confident the moon landings were real and see conspiracy theories as unfounded.
Cautious moderates who accept the moon landings likely happened but have some residual doubts about official narratives. They lean toward the mainstream view but aren't entirely certain.
Conspiracy-minded skeptics who believe the moon landings were faked as part of Cold War propaganda. They distrust government and institutional claims about major historical events.
Undecided fence-sitters who lack strong conviction either way and are genuinely uncertain about whether the landings were real or fabricated.
Committed conspiracy theorists who are certain the moon landings were faked and see this as obvious evidence of government deception and media complicity.

Skeptical majority who trust scientific consensus on vaccines. These people view vaccine safety concerns as exaggerated and believe health authorities are generally reliable, though they may acknowledge room for improvement in transparency.

Cautious moderates who have some concerns about vaccine safety but don't believe in deliberate cover-ups. They think there may be legitimate debates about vaccine effects that deserve more public discussion, without assuming intentional deception.

Conspiracy-minded believers who are convinced that governments and pharmaceutical companies are actively hiding vaccine dangers. They see this as part of broader patterns of institutional deception similar to other cover-ups.

Uncertain fence-sitters who lack strong convictions either way. They're unsure whether to trust official narratives about vaccines and haven't formed firm opinions on whether harmful effects are being hidden.

Anti-establishment skeptics who distrust institutions generally and assume hidden agendas are likely. They view vaccine safety claims with suspicion as part of their broader rejection of official narratives.
Skeptical of official narratives across domains. Believes Trump's team likely coordinated with Russia based on distrust of establishment accounts and pattern-matching to other conspiracies.
Moderately critical of Trump and receptive to allegations of Russian interference, viewing it as plausible given geopolitical tensions and some reported evidence.
Mainstream centrists who see the Russia allegations as unproven or exaggerated, preferring to await definitive evidence before accepting the claim.
Strong Trump supporters or those skeptical of anti-Trump narratives who reject the Russian coordination claim as a politically motivated hoax.
Genuinely uncertain or disengaged from US politics, lacking strong priors about Trump, Russia, or election interference.

Skeptical of US institutions and geopolitical narratives. This group tends to believe that powerful actors manipulate world events, and sees Trump-Russia coordination as plausible given broader patterns of hidden influence they perceive.
Moderately critical but cautious. They have some doubts about official accounts and think Trump-Russia coordination is possible, but aren't fully convinced without stronger evidence.

Mainstream consensus followers. They accept the general Western narrative about Trump and Russia based on media coverage and official investigations, viewing the coordination claim as probably or definitely false.
Strong institutional trust. They firmly reject claims of Trump-Russia coordination as conspiracy thinking, viewing such allegations as politically motivated attacks rather than credible concerns.

Genuinely uncertain or disengaged. They lack strong conviction on this geopolitical question and prefer to withhold judgment, either due to information gaps or skepticism toward all sides of the debate.
Mainstream skeptics of conspiracy theories who accept established historical accounts. They reject Holocaust denial and view it as morally reprehensible pseudohistory.

Cautious moderates who are generally skeptical of official narratives but recognize the Holocaust as historically documented. They may have some doubts about specific details but reject the core denial.

Conspiracy-minded individuals who distrust mainstream accounts across multiple domains and are receptive to revisionist historical claims. They tend to view the Holocaust narrative as potentially exaggerated.

Uncertain respondents with limited engagement on this specific historical question who lack strong convictions either way. They may default to 'don't know' or express mild skepticism without firm commitment.
Committed Holocaust deniers who actively believe the official account is a deliberate lie and that victim numbers have been systematically inflated for political purposes.
Skeptical of official narratives and prone to conspiracy thinking. This group believes governments routinely hide truth and sees 9/11 as likely involving US government involvement or foreknowledge.
Moderately trusting of mainstream accounts but open to alternative explanations. They find some 9/11 conspiracy claims plausible but aren't fully convinced the US government orchestrated the attacks.
Mainstream believers in the official 9/11 account. They accept that al-Qaeda terrorists carried out the attacks and reject claims of US government involvement as unfounded.
Highly skeptical of conspiracy theories and strongly defend the official narrative. They view 9/11 conspiracy claims as thoroughly debunked and see them as disrespectful to victims.
Genuinely uncertain or disengaged from the question. They lack strong conviction either way and may not have formed a clear opinion on 9/11 conspiracy claims.
Vaccine skeptics who believe health authorities are concealing vaccine dangers. They distrust institutional narratives and see parallels with other hidden truths.
Cautious moderates who think there might be some suppressed information about vaccine side effects, though they're uncertain about the extent of any cover-up.
Mainstream consensus followers who accept that vaccine safety is well-documented and publicly available, viewing claims of hidden harms as unfounded.
Agnostic fence-sitters who lack strong conviction either way and don't feel they have enough reliable information to judge the claim.
Strong institutional defenders who are confident that vaccine safety is rigorously monitored and that any suggestion of deliberate concealment is false.

Mainstream sceptics who distrust official narratives but apply critical thinking selectively. They believe Trump-Russia collusion claims warrant serious investigation based on media reporting, though they may have doubts about the extent of 'knowing' coordination.
Anti-Trump progressives who view the Russia interference narrative as credible and see Trump's team as likely complicit in deliberate coordination with Russian actors.
Conservative Trump supporters who reject the Russia collusion narrative entirely as a hoax or exaggeration, viewing it as politically motivated.
Cautious moderates who acknowledge Russian interference occurred but remain uncertain whether Trump's team knowingly coordinated with Russia, seeing the evidence as ambiguous.
Disengaged citizens with low political interest who lack strong views on this question and are uncertain about the facts surrounding Trump-Russia allegations.
Skeptical moderates who trust mainstream health institutions and scientific consensus on vaccine safety, viewing claims of hidden vaccine harms as unfounded conspiracy theories.
Cautious believers who think there may be some truth to concerns about vaccine side effects being downplayed, though they're not entirely convinced of deliberate deception.
Convinced skeptics who strongly believe vaccine safety information is being suppressed and that governments and pharmaceutical companies are hiding harmful effects from the public.
Uncertain fence-sitters who lack strong convictions either way and are genuinely unsure whether vaccine safety concerns are being deliberately hidden.

Pragmatic doubters who acknowledge some vaccine hesitancy exists in Nigeria due to past medical mistrust and colonial history, making them receptive to concerns about hidden information even if not fully convinced.
Skeptical rationalists who reject conspiracy theories across the board. They see no credible evidence for a secret world-controlling group and view such claims as unfounded speculation.
Cautious doubters who are uncertain about hidden power structures but lean toward skepticism. They acknowledge the possibility of secret influence but find it unproven and unlikely.

Conspiracy-curious moderates who think it's plausible that a hidden group controls world events, though they're not fully convinced. They see enough irregularities in world affairs to keep an open mind.
Convinced believers who are fairly sure a secret elite group rules the world behind the scenes. They see patterns of hidden control across governments and major institutions.
Uncertain fence-sitters who genuinely don't know what to think about secret world control. They lack strong convictions either way and need more information to decide.

Pragmatic safety evaluators who focus on literal harm: These workers assess content primarily on whether it directly causes physical, psychological, or social harm. They see a casual conversation about cocktail preferences as harmless small talk with no connection to group-based discrimination.

Moderate acceptors who disagree with feeling ashamed of gay family members but may hold some traditional reservations. They believe in live-and-let-live without necessarily being strongly activist.
Conflicted traditionalists who are uncertain about their feelings, neither fully accepting nor rejecting LGBTQ+ family members. They struggle between evolving social norms and conservative values.
Conservative believers who would feel some shame about having a gay family member, rooted in religious or traditional family values that remain important to their worldview.
Strong traditionalists who would feel significant shame, viewing homosexuality as incompatible with their deeply held religious or cultural beliefs about family and morality.
Religious traditionalists who maintain strong Catholic faith and see religious identity as central to Polish culture and personal identity
Secular pragmatists who do not identify with any religion but respect religious traditions and are not actively hostile to faith
Indifferent non-believers who have little interest in religion and view it as irrelevant to their daily lives
Spiritual seekers who may not align with institutional religion but maintain some personal spiritual beliefs or practices
Active atheists or anti-religious individuals who consciously reject religious identity and may be critical of religious influence
Politically disengaged working-class people who rarely participate in any civic activities, viewing petitions as ineffective or irrelevant to their daily lives.
Socially conscious individuals with some education or exposure to activism who occasionally sign petitions on issues they care about, particularly those affecting their community or family.
Religiously motivated people who sign petitions aligned with Catholic or Christian values, such as those opposing abortion or defending religious freedoms.
Younger or more progressive members who support social causes like LGBTQ+ rights and environmental protection, and see petitions as a legitimate form of activism.
Highly engaged civic participants who regularly sign petitions across multiple causes and view them as an important democratic tool.

Progressive-minded seniors who strongly reject traditional stigma around homosexuality and would feel no shame whatsoever if a family member were gay; they view sexual orientation as a personal matter deserving full acceptance.
Tolerant moderates who accept homosexuality as normal and would not feel ashamed of a gay family member, though they may have some reservations about certain issues like adoption rights.

Conflicted middle-grounders who are uncertain about their feelings on this issue, neither strongly rejecting nor embracing the idea, reflecting generational tension between traditional values and modern acceptance.
Traditional conservatives who maintain some discomfort with homosexuality and would experience some shame if a close family member were gay, rooted in religious or cultural values.
Strong traditionalists who firmly believe homosexuality conflicts with their values and would feel significant shame about a gay family member, representing the most resistant segment.

Civically engaged retirees who remain active in their communities. They view petition-signing as a natural extension of their lifelong civic participation and are likely to have signed petitions in the past year.

Moderately involved citizens who occasionally engage in civic activities but are selective about which causes they support. They may sign petitions for issues they care deeply about, but don't make it a regular practice.

Politically cautious older adults who prefer traditional forms of engagement or no engagement at all. They view petition-signing as somewhat ineffective or prefer to express their views through voting alone.

Digitally hesitant seniors who are uncomfortable with modern petition formats, particularly online petitions, even if they might support the underlying causes. They rarely sign petitions due to practical barriers.

Disengaged or apathetic individuals who see little point in petition-signing or other forms of activism. They believe individual actions make no meaningful difference and prefer to focus on personal matters.
Devout Catholics who view religious identity as central to their Polish heritage and personal identity. Religion is an important part of daily life and community belonging.
Culturally Catholic Poles who identify with the religion as part of their national and family tradition, but practice it less actively or regularly.
Secular or non-religious individuals who have moved away from religious identification, viewing it as less relevant to their lives despite Poland's strong Catholic culture.
Agnostic or doubtful individuals who are uncertain about religious belief and may have complicated relationships with the Catholic Church's authority and teachings.
Active members of other Christian denominations or minority religions who identify with their specific faith community rather than Catholicism.

Progressive urbanites who strongly reject traditional stigma. They would firmly disagree that they'd feel ashamed of a gay family member, viewing such feelings as outdated and contrary to personal freedom.
Socially liberal mainstream Russians who accept LGBTQ+ people in principle. They would disagree with feeling ashamed, though they may hold some traditional reservations in practice.
Traditionalists with conservative values who feel conflicted. They might agree they would feel some shame, reflecting deeply ingrained cultural and possibly religious norms about family honor.
Religious conservatives who strongly agree they would feel ashamed, viewing homosexuality as incompatible with their faith and family values.
Ambivalent middle-ground Russians who neither strongly agree nor disagree, uncertain how they would actually feel in such a situation.
Pragmatic acceptors: Legally married Austrians who view cohabitation without marriage as a normal, acceptable lifestyle choice that doesn't require their approval or disapproval.
Neutral observers: Married Austrians who neither approve nor disapprove of unmarried cohabitation, seeing it as a personal choice that falls outside their moral judgment.
Traditional skeptics: Married Austrians who disapprove of cohabitation without marriage, viewing legal marriage as the proper foundation for shared living arrangements.
Strong traditionalists: Married Austrians who strongly disapprove of unmarried cohabitation, seeing it as contrary to their values and social norms.
Enthusiastic progressives: Married Austrians who strongly approve of cohabitation without marriage as a valid expression of personal freedom and relationship autonomy.

Non-unionized workers with limited civic engagement. These individuals have never joined a trade union and show minimal participation in collective action or organizational work, reflecting the 92-96% who don't engage in association work.

Former union members from earlier career stages. These people were previously unionized but are no longer active members, possibly due to job changes, retirement, or shifting priorities as they aged through their careers.

Currently active union members in traditional sectors. These individuals maintain current union membership, likely working in more unionized industries or sectors where collective representation remains relevant and valued.
Skeptical non-joiners with individualistic views. These people consciously reject union membership, preferring to handle workplace issues independently rather than through collective organizations.
Unaware or disengaged workers. These individuals have limited knowledge of union options or simply haven't considered membership as relevant to their work situation.
Politically disengaged workers with limited education and resources. They rarely participate in any civic activities including boycotts, viewing such actions as irrelevant to their daily struggles.

Conservative traditionalists with strong religious beliefs and nationalist views. They are skeptical of consumer activism and boycotts, seeing them as Western-influenced or destabilizing to social order.
Educated urban professionals and trade union members with some civic engagement. They occasionally participate in boycotts when issues align with their values or union positions.
Socially conscious younger individuals or those with exposure to international ideas. They are more likely to support boycotts as a form of consumer activism and social responsibility.
Active civil society participants with higher education and professional development. They regularly engage in boycotts as part of broader civic and political participation.
Progressive urbanites who embrace modern living arrangements. They have likely cohabited with partners and see it as a normal, acceptable part of contemporary life.
Pragmatic moderates who may have cohabited or considered it without strong moral objections. They view cohabitation as a personal choice that doesn't conflict with their values.

Traditional Catholics and conservatives who disapprove of cohabitation on moral or religious grounds. They have not lived with unmarried partners and believe marriage should precede shared living arrangements.
Older traditionalists with strong family values who never cohabited and view it as improper, though they may be somewhat resigned to its prevalence in modern society.
Indifferent pragmatists who neither strongly approve nor disapprove of cohabitation. They may or may not have experienced it themselves but don't see it as a significant moral issue.
Secular progressives with strong liberal values who have rejected religious affiliation entirely, viewing religion as incompatible with modern, evidence-based thinking.
Cultural Catholics or nominal believers who maintain religious identity as part of Belgian/European heritage and tradition, even if they don't practice regularly.
Committed religious practitioners from Catholic or other Christian denominations who actively identify with their faith and consider it central to their identity.
Agnostics or spiritual-but-not-religious individuals who are uncertain about religious claims but haven't completely rejected the possibility of religious belonging.
Members of non-Christian religious communities (Muslim, Jewish, Buddhist, etc.) who identify with their specific religious denomination.
Pragmatic acceptors who have cohabited themselves and see it as a normal modern choice; they approve of cohabitation without marriage.
Neutral moderates who neither approve nor disapprove of cohabitation; they view it as a personal choice without strong moral judgment.
Traditional skeptics who disapprove of cohabitation without marriage on moral or religious grounds, preferring formal commitment.
Cautious conservatives who strongly disapprove of unmarried cohabitation as contrary to traditional family values.
Enthusiastic progressives who strongly approve of cohabitation as a valid lifestyle choice reflecting personal freedom and modern values.

Engaged civic participants - typically employed professionals or pensioners with stable incomes who actively participate in community organizations and associations as part of their regular civic engagement.
Time-constrained workers - employed individuals coping on their income who lack the time or energy to participate in organizational work outside their primary employment.
Comfortable retirees - pensioners living comfortably who have the time and inclination to volunteer or work with associations, viewing it as a meaningful use of their retirement.
Socially isolated or disengaged - individuals (whether employed or not) who feel disconnected from community institutions and see little relevance in organizational participation to their lives.
Financially stressed non-participants - those struggling financially who prioritize survival and immediate needs over voluntary organizational work, lacking both time and resources.

Progressive cohabitants: Young to middle-aged Finns who strongly approve of unmarried cohabitation and have personal experience living with partners without marriage. They view this as a normal, accepted lifestyle choice.

Pragmatic acceptors: Moderate centrists who approve or are neutral about cohabitation and have lived with partners unmarried. They see it as a practical arrangement that doesn't require moral judgment.

Cautious traditionalists: Center-right Finns who are somewhat uncomfortable with unmarried cohabitation but haven't personally experienced it, viewing marriage as preferable though not condemning alternatives.
Committed traditionalists: More conservative individuals who disapprove of cohabitation without marriage and have never lived with unmarried partners, preferring formal marital commitment.
Neutral observers: Finns with no strong views on cohabitation who haven't lived with unmarried partners, remaining indifferent to the lifestyle choice.
Progressive urban women who strongly reject traditional stigma around homosexuality and would feel no shame whatsoever if a family member were gay, viewing such feelings as outdated prejudice.

Socially liberal women who disagree with the statement but may have some residual discomfort, representing those who intellectually support LGBTQ+ rights while not being as vocally passionate about it.

Moderate women who are genuinely uncertain about their feelings on this personal question, neither strongly rejecting nor accepting the idea of shame, reflecting ambivalence between modern values and traditional upbringing.
Conservative women who would feel some degree of shame or discomfort if a close family member were gay, holding more traditional views despite living in a modernizing society.
Strongly traditional women who would feel significant shame, representing those with deeply held conservative or religious values that conflict with accepting homosexuality in their own family.
Conservative traditionalists with strong family values who believe adoption rights should remain with heterosexual couples only, reflecting traditional views on family structure.
Moderate conservatives who have reservations about same-sex adoption but are not strongly opposed, viewing it as a departure from tradition without being deeply committed to preventing it.
Pragmatic middle-grounders who are uncertain about the issue and see valid arguments on both sides, preferring to remain neutral on this socially divisive question.
Progressive supporters who believe in equal rights for same-sex couples and see no reason to deny them adoption rights based on sexual orientation.
Strong equality advocates who firmly support same-sex adoption rights as a matter of principle and non-discrimination, viewing opposition as outdated prejudice.
Comfortable wage earners: Employed professionals and dual-income households with stable salaries who feel financially secure and are living comfortably on their present income.
Coping middle class: Salaried workers and self-employed individuals managing adequately but without significant surplus, coping on their present income without major financial stress.
Struggling workers: Lower-wage employees or those with irregular self-employment income who find it difficult to make ends meet on their current household income.
Pensioners: Retired individuals living on fixed pensions who vary widely—some comfortable, others finding it very difficult depending on pension adequacy and savings.
Severely strained households: Those facing very difficult financial circumstances, including unemployed individuals, those on benefits, or households with unexpected hardships.
Daily digital natives who are constantly connected across devices for work and personal life, representing the growing segment of Italians integrated into the digital economy.
Regular internet users who access the web most days for both professional and leisure purposes, comfortable with digital tools but not necessarily always online.
Moderate users who go online a few times a week for specific needs like email, news, or social media, representing those with selective digital engagement.
Occasional internet users who only use devices sporadically, often older or less digitally oriented individuals who maintain limited online presence.
Non-users or those who never use the internet, a small but persistent segment in Italy reflecting digital exclusion among certain demographics.

Progressive cohabiters who have lived with partners without marriage and strongly approve of this lifestyle choice. They view cohabitation as a normal, acceptable alternative to marriage and likely support other progressive social values like LGBTQ+ rights.

Pragmatic acceptors who have lived with partners without marriage and are comfortable with this arrangement, though they may be more neutral or moderately approving rather than strongly enthusiastic about it as a lifestyle choice.

Traditional non-cohabiters who have not lived with partners outside of marriage and disapprove of cohabitation, viewing marriage as the proper framework for partnership. They tend to be more conservative on social issues generally.

Neutral fence-sitters who have not lived with partners without marriage but hold neither strong approval nor disapproval of cohabitation, reflecting the substantial middle ground in Dutch society on this issue.

Conflicted individuals who may have cohabited but express ambivalence about it, or who disapprove of cohabitation despite having experienced it, suggesting some tension between their actions and stated values.

Engaged civic participants - typically better educated, regularly online, religiously affiliated, and actively involved in community organizations. They see organizational work as a natural extension of their social and civic responsibilities.

Socially connected but organizationally inactive - comfortable with their lives, moderate internet users, often religious, but they prefer informal social networks over formal organizational commitments.
Economically stressed and withdrawn - struggling financially, less frequent internet use, they lack time and resources for organizational involvement and tend to focus on immediate household needs.

Young digital natives with limited civic engagement - daily internet users, but not particularly motivated by organizational participation; they may engage through informal online communities rather than traditional associations.
Skeptical non-participants - whether due to distrust of institutions, lack of interest, or competing priorities, they simply do not see value in working within formal organizations.
Engaged centrists and moderate progressives who feel connected to mainstream center-left or centrist parties that align with their socially liberal values on cohabitation and childlessness.
Pragmatic non-aligned citizens who hold progressive social views but feel disconnected from all political parties, viewing them as insufficiently representative of their interests.
Left-leaning activists and union members who identify strongly with left-wing or socialist parties that champion workers' rights and progressive social policies.
Conservative or religious-minded individuals who feel closer to center-right or traditional parties, though they represent a minority within this socially liberal group.
Apolitical or deeply skeptical citizens who reject partisan identification entirely, viewing political parties as fundamentally disconnected from their lived experience.

Progressive liberals who strongly reject traditional stigma around homosexuality. They would emphatically disagree with feeling ashamed of a gay family member, viewing such shame as fundamentally wrong.
Socially liberal but somewhat cautious individuals who disagree with the statement but without the strongest conviction. They accept gay family members but may have some residual discomfort.
Neutral or conflicted people who haven't fully formed their views on this personal emotional question. They neither strongly embrace nor reject the idea of feeling ashamed.
Conservative individuals who hold traditional values and would experience some genuine discomfort or shame about having a gay family member, though they may not express this strongly.
Strongly traditional people who believe homosexuality conflicts with their values and would openly admit to feeling ashamed of a gay family member.
Digitally active retirees who remain engaged with learning and self-improvement. They see continued education as valuable for staying mentally sharp and relevant, even in retirement.
Traditionally-minded older retirees with limited internet use who view their working years as complete and see no need for further professional development or skill-building.

Selective learners interested in specific hobbies or personal interests rather than work-related skills. They may attend lectures on topics like history, culture, or health that appeal to them personally.
Health-conscious and socially engaged retirees who participate in community courses and wellness programs as part of an active retirement lifestyle, viewing education as part of staying connected.
Financially or physically limited retirees with barriers to participation, whether due to mobility issues, economic constraints, or lack of accessible educational opportunities in their area.
Traditional conservatives who strongly disapprove of unmarried cohabitation and childbearing outside marriage, viewing these as violations of family values and social norms.
Moderate traditionalists who disapprove but are not strongly opposed, uncomfortable with the trend but accepting it as increasingly common in modern society.
Pragmatic moderates who neither approve nor disapprove, viewing unmarried partnerships and childbearing as a personal choice without strong moral judgment either way.
Progressive liberals who approve of unmarried couples having children together, seeing it as a legitimate family arrangement based on love and commitment rather than legal status.
Strong progressives who strongly approve, viewing marriage as optional and believing that children can thrive in unmarried partnerships with equal validity to traditional families.
Women from traditional working-class families where mothers stayed home to raise children, reflecting common post-communist family patterns of the 1980s-90s.
Women whose mothers worked as employees in state enterprises or public sector jobs, the dominant employment model during the communist era in Poland.
Women from small business or farming backgrounds where mothers were self-employed, particularly in rural areas or family enterprises.
Women who experienced family disruption, with mothers who were deceased or absent during their childhood.
Women uncertain about their mother's exact employment status or from families where this information was not clearly communicated.
Daily digital workers: Professionals who rely on internet for their paid work and use it constantly throughout the day for both professional and personal purposes.
Regular evening users: Working people who use the internet most days after work hours for news, social media, and personal tasks, but not constantly.
Moderate weekly users: Employed individuals who access the internet a few times a week for specific needs like banking, shopping, or occasional browsing, but don't rely on it daily.
Occasional pragmatists: Workers who use the internet only occasionally for essential tasks and prefer offline activities, reflecting lower digital engagement.
Digital abstainers: A small segment of the working population who rarely or never use the internet, either by choice or due to limited access.
Working-class individuals with stable employment who have joined or currently belong to a trade union to protect their labor rights and negotiate better working conditions.
Former union members from earlier career stages who were previously unionized but are no longer active members, either due to job changes or retirement.
Self-employed workers, small business owners, and informal sector workers who have never been union members and see little relevance of unions to their work situation.
Young people and those in precarious or temporary employment who lack awareness of union benefits or face barriers to unionization in their current jobs.
Older workers and retirees with limited formal employment history who never had the opportunity or need to join a union during their working lives.

Pragmatic centrists who feel connected to established parties. These individuals have moderate incomes, stable employment histories (often union members), and see value in aligning with a mainstream political party that represents their interests.

Disengaged skeptics with weak party affiliation. They struggle financially, feel disconnected from traditional institutions, and don't feel particularly close to any political party despite Hungary's polarized landscape.
Ideologically committed party loyalists. These people have strong convictions about which party best represents their values and actively identify with a particular political movement.
Socially conservative traditionalists aligned with religious values. They belong to a religious denomination and feel closer to parties that reflect their moral and cultural worldview.
Progressive independents who reject party politics. They hold liberal social views (accepting of non-marital partnerships) and deliberately distance themselves from formal party identification.
Rural agricultural workers and small farmers with traditional employment patterns who have never engaged with formal union structures, viewing them as irrelevant to their way of life.
Older residents who worked in industrial or public sector jobs during their careers and were union members, but are now retired and no longer active.
Younger, more educated villagers with professional or service sector jobs who see limited value in union membership given the small-scale, informal nature of rural employment.
Small business owners and self-employed artisans who actively avoid union involvement due to their independent economic status and skepticism of collective organizations.
Factory or construction workers commuting from the village who maintain current union membership as a practical protection for their formal employment.
Progressive urbanites with liberal values who approve of cohabitation and have likely lived with partners themselves. They see cohabitation as a normal, acceptable lifestyle choice.
Pragmatic moderates who are neutral or mildly approving of cohabitation and may have personal experience with it. They view it as a reasonable option without strong moral judgment.
Traditional conservatives who disapprove of cohabitation on moral or religious grounds and have not lived with unmarried partners. They believe marriage should precede cohabitation.
Socially conservative but accepting individuals who personally disapprove but recognize it as increasingly common. They may have limited personal experience with cohabitation.
Younger or more secular Finns with strong approval of cohabitation who view marriage as optional. They are likely to have lived with partners and see it as the natural progression of relationships.
Pragmatic mainstream workers who trust Swiss institutions and regulatory processes. They view vaccination as a straightforward public health measure and will get vaccinated when available.

Cautious but compliant citizens who have some hesitations about vaccine speed or necessity but ultimately defer to national health authorities. They will likely get vaccinated but may wait to see how rollout proceeds.
Skeptical individuals who distrust rapid vaccine development or government health mandates, preferring to rely on natural immunity or alternative approaches. They are unlikely to get vaccinated.
Health-conscious early adopters who actively follow scientific developments and are eager to get vaccinated as soon as possible. They see vaccination as both personal and civic responsibility.
Disengaged citizens with low civic participation who haven't thought much about vaccination and may not follow through unless vaccination becomes mandatory or highly inconvenient to avoid.
Engaged professionals and lifelong learners who actively pursue continuous skill development through courses and conferences, viewing professional growth as essential in a changing economy.
Moderately active workers who occasionally take training courses when directly required by their employer or when they identify a specific skill gap, but don't prioritize ongoing learning.
Established professionals in stable positions who feel their skills are already sufficient and see little need for additional formal training at this stage of their careers.
Less digitally engaged individuals who are skeptical about formal training programs and prefer learning through practical experience or informal methods rather than structured courses.
Recently retired or semi-retired workers who have largely stepped back from workforce participation and therefore have minimal motivation to invest in work-related skill development.
Healthy pragmatists who rarely need medical care and see long waiting lists as a system problem that doesn't affect them personally.
Occasional healthcare users who have experienced some wait times but managed to get treatment eventually, viewing delays as frustrating but acceptable.
Regular healthcare consumers who have directly experienced significant waiting list delays and see this as a serious accessibility issue in the Australian system.
Chronic condition patients who depend on timely medical treatment and have been negatively impacted by long waits, viewing this as a critical healthcare system failure.
Skeptical or uncertain respondents who are unsure whether their healthcare delays were due to waiting lists specifically or other factors.
Devout believers in Catholic faith who accept miracles as real manifestations of divine power, common in rural Philippine communities with strong church presence.
Pragmatic believers who think miracles probably happen but are cautious about claims, viewing them as rare and requiring strong evidence.
Skeptics who doubt miracles occur in the modern world, attributing unusual events to natural causes or coincidence rather than divine intervention.
Uncertain villagers who lack strong conviction either way, influenced by traditional beliefs but also exposed to secular thinking, unable to decide confidently.
Outright disbelievers who reject miracles as superstition incompatible with rational understanding of how the world works.
Non-religious secular individuals who don't follow any religion and view the question as not applicable to their lives.
Committed religious believers who follow a religion and genuinely believe their faith treats men and women equally, reflecting their personal experience or theological understanding.
Religious practitioners who acknowledge that while they follow a religion, they recognize it treats men better than women in practice or doctrine.
Spiritual but non-religious individuals who don't follow a formal religion but hold spiritual beliefs and find the question not directly relevant to their worldview.
Uncertain or conflicted respondents who follow a religion but are unsure how to characterize gender treatment within it, or who see it as complex and context-dependent.
Secular skeptics who reject religious concepts entirely. They don't believe in God, don't believe in heaven, hell, or miracles, and similarly reject the idea of life after death as wishful thinking.
Agnostic doubters uncertain about metaphysical claims. They're unsure about God's existence and remain genuinely undecided about afterlife, heaven, and hell, seeing these as unknowable questions.
Spiritual but not religious believers who accept a Higher Power and some spiritual concepts like miracles, but are uncertain or skeptical about traditional afterlife doctrines like heaven and hell.

Moderate believers with some faith in God and openness to spiritual possibilities. They probably believe in life after death and heaven, though with some doubts, and are less certain about hell and miracles.
Committed religious believers who have strong faith in God and are confident in life after death. They tend to believe in heaven, though views on hell and miracles vary among this group.

Working-class residents with modest incomes who see themselves as struggling to get by; they place themselves in the lower-middle range (3-5) as they feel economically squeezed despite having stable employment.
Lower-income pensioners and unemployed individuals who have experienced economic hardship; they tend to place themselves at the bottom (1-3) as they feel left behind by society.

Small business owners, skilled tradespeople, and local professionals who feel moderately successful; they place themselves in the middle-to-upper range (6-7) as they have achieved some stability and respect in their small communities.

Young educated people (teachers, engineers, doctors) who have professional status but limited wealth in small-town contexts; they place themselves in the middle range (5-6) as they have education and respect but not significant material wealth.
A small segment of wealthy local elites (business owners, regional officials) who place themselves at the top (8-10); they are confident in their superior social and economic position.
Secular materialists who reject both organized religion and spiritual belief systems. They view themselves as rational and evidence-based, seeing no need for religious or spiritual frameworks.

Pragmatic non-religious individuals who maintain some spiritual sensibilities or openness to transcendent experiences without committing to formal religion. They appreciate spiritual concepts while remaining skeptical of institutional religion.

Traditional religious practitioners, often Buddhist or Taoist, who actively follow religious practices and consider themselves both religious and spiritual. They engage with scripture and maintain faith in divine or transcendent forces.

Lapsed or culturally religious people who were raised in a religious tradition but no longer actively practice or believe. They may retain some spiritual inclinations from their upbringing but don't identify as religious.

Undecided or conflicted individuals who struggle to categorize themselves clearly on religious and spiritual dimensions. They may be exploring their beliefs or find the categories themselves problematic.
Secular skeptics who don't believe in God and are skeptical of religious miracles. They see miracles as unlikely or explainable through natural causes.
Agnostic fence-sitters who are uncertain about religious matters generally and remain undecided about whether miracles occur. They find the question difficult to answer definitively.
Moderate believers who accept God's existence and think miracles are probably real, though they're not absolutely certain. They see miracles as possible but not inevitable.
Traditional believers who have always believed in God and are confident that religious miracles definitely happen. They view miracles as evidence of divine intervention.
Pragmatic non-believers who don't believe in God now and are skeptical of miracles, though they may not be completely certain. They lean toward natural explanations.
Committed environmentalists who actively engage in environmental causes through petitions and other advocacy; they recycle consistently and see environmental action as a personal responsibility.
Moderately engaged citizens who care about environmental issues and recycle regularly, but haven't taken the step of signing petitions; they support environmental causes passively.
Casual recyclers with mixed environmental engagement who may have signed a petition on an issue they felt strongly about, but don't systematically participate in environmental activism.
Skeptical or disengaged individuals who recycle minimally and see environmental petitions as ineffective or not worth their time; they tend toward inaction on these issues.
Religiously-minded people who view environmental stewardship through a faith lens and may sign petitions as an extension of their values, though their participation varies widely.

Traditional Catholics and conservative believers who view same-sex relations as morally wrong, grounded in religious teachings they take seriously. They tend to answer 'Always wrong' or 'Almost always wrong.'

Religiously moderate people who believe in God but hold more nuanced views, seeing same-sex relations as acceptable even if their faith tradition has reservations. They lean toward 'Not wrong at all' or 'Wrong only sometimes.'

Secular or non-religious Lithuanians who don't base their morality on religious doctrine and view same-sex relations as a personal matter with no moral dimension. They clearly answer 'Not wrong at all.'

Uncertain middle-ground people who are conflicted between traditional values they were raised with and more liberal modern attitudes, or who simply haven't formed a strong opinion. They choose 'Can't choose' or 'Wrong only sometimes.'

Young or urban-influenced Lithuanians with progressive views who actively reject traditional condemnation of same-sex relations and see them as fully acceptable. They answer 'Not wrong at all' with conviction.
Established middle-class professionals with stable employment who rely on employer-based insurance, often supplemented with private coverage for better access and shorter waiting times.
Standard public insurance holders who are satisfied with Germany's national health system and see no need for additional private coverage.
Affluent individuals who prefer comprehensive private insurance or a combination of private and public coverage to ensure premium care and minimal waiting periods.
